title: Keep Nil
passages:
Sol handed the wheel to Dey without looking back. "Hold her off the pier," she said. "Don't let her drift into the channel while I'm gone."

Dey was still wet from hauling Nia up the service trunk, his hair plastered to his forehead, one hand wrapped in a rag from the salt burns. "You want me to steer this tub with a surge coming and your credit in the gutter?" he said. "Fine. But if we swing into the gate, I'm telling Quill you ordered it."

"She can't stop a boat with words," Sol said. She tucked the Marrow's bond into the oilskin pouch at her belt and turned for the steel stair.

The Kettle's low gate was a rib of rusted iron sunk into the drowned coast, its lock teeth half-lifted against the incoming tide. Storm season had the water chopping at the pilings, and the arcology loomed behind it like a tooth that hadn't fallen out yet. Sol's boots rang on the stair, each step pulling her higher above the waterline where the good seats were. The bond felt thin against her hip, paper and wax, the Marrow's surety written out to Pru Quill's berth book. Enough to buy six berths, if the count wasn't full. If the warden would open the shutter.

At the top, the dock-warden's box hung over the channel like a crow's nest built by accountants. Glass windows, steel frame, a single lantern burning inside. Sol climbed the last rung and planted her palms on the sill.

The shutter was down.

She knocked once, hard. "Quill. Open up."

No answer. Through the glass she could see the berth book lying on the counter, thick and leather-bound, a heavy chain run through its cover and looped around a bolt in the frame. A second chain locked the shutter itself, padlocked at the hasp. The little window in the door was open just a crack, barely wide enough for a voice, and a slip of paper had been wedged in it.

COUNT FULL, the slip said in Quill's sharp hand. NO BERTHS BEFORE SPRING.

Sol's fingers closed on the oilskin pouch. The bond didn't crinkle. It had been pressed flat by days in her coat, the ink black and certain. The Marrow's surety. Her boat. All of it, offered for six highland berths before the storm bell sealed the channel for the season.

She knocked again. "Quill. I'm not leaving until you look at it."

A bell sounded somewhere below, deep and slow—the storm bell marking the pause before the lock teeth dropped. Through the glass, Sol saw movement inside. Not Quill. A shadow shifting behind the counter, then stillness.

The chain on the book gleamed in the lantern light. The count was full. Six names, or seven, or however many Quill had squeezed in before the tide turned. Sol's name wasn't among them. The Marrow wasn't either. She had come to trade a boat for a future, and the warden had shut the door.

She set her shoulder against the shutter. It didn't move. The padlock was new, the steel cold under her palm.

"Open it," Sol said, her voice low. "I know you're in there."

The lock teeth began to turn below her with a groan of metal on metal, the gate sealing itself against the rising water. She had minutes, maybe less, before the channel locked and no boat—hers or anyone else's—could pass until spring.

The chain through the shutter's hasp had a hand's width of slack in it. Sol hooked two fingers under the shutter and pulled until the links went tight, and the steel came up three inches and stopped.

Quill's eye filled the gap. Then the rest of her face, green-lit from the lantern behind her, wearing the look of a woman who had been awake for two tides and had decided to make that everybody's problem.

"Four words," Quill said. "I put four words on a slip for you and you came back with your shoulder."

"Read this instead." Sol flattened the oilskin on the sill and fed the bond through the gap. Wax, ribbon, the *Marrow* written out in a clerk's careful hand. "The hull against six highland berths. Surety means you take the boat if I default, cut her up for scrap, and the rest of the debt stays yours. That's a good trade and you know it."

"I know what surety is. I write them." Quill didn't touch the paper. "It's forfeit."

"It's sealed."

"Forfeit and sealed aren't opposites, captain." She said it the way another woman would read a depth off a line. "Your bond died at slack water on the ninth, when two children were standing on your deck where the Factor's twelve thousand should have been. Not void. *Forfeit.* The difference is the whole of it."

Below, the Marrow's engine note climbed and held. Sol could hear Dey swearing at the throttle in the flat, patient voice he used when he was frightened and wouldn't say so. She had that hour now, or the account of it — her own voice off a slate, calm, saying the children come up first. She could recite it start to finish. She could not remember standing inside it.

"Then price the hull," she said. "Scrap value. Now. Tonight."

"The hull isn't mine to price and you'd not like the number." Quill's chin came up. "You're not buying with a boat anyway. You're buying with a story about metal under the Line, and I've heard that one off every crew that's ever come up my stair wet."

"I'm not asking for credit. I'm asking you to write six names."

"Then write them yourself." Quill nodded at the chained book. "Pen's inside. So's the tide table, the count, and forty-one people who paid in coin, in medicine, in a son's indenture, in a hand. Nothing you set on this counter moves that number. Not wax, not paper, not brass."

Sol took the sounding lead off her belt — her mother's, worn smooth, a lump of gray metal on four fathoms of line — and laid it in the gap. Quill looked at it for exactly as long as it took to be sure.

"That's a good lead," she said. "It isn't a berth."

"Everyone has a price, warden."

"You've been talking to the Factor's people." Quill's mouth flattened. "I don't have prices. I have a book. Prices are for people who can bend a thing and still sleep."

"Forty-one," Sol said. "You've never been under forty meters in your life, and you'll stand there and tell me what my crew forgets down there like it's a matter of tidy handwriting."

"I've never been below the Line and I don't intend to be." Quill's voice didn't rise, which was worse. "Down there a man forgets his mother's face and blames the water. Up here we call that not writing things down."

Sol put both palms flat on the sill, in the three-inch gap, and left them there. The lock teeth turned another notch under her boots and the whole stair shuddered, and out on the black water the Marrow's horn gave one short blast — Dey, saying *hurry* in the only language he had left that the salt hadn't taken.

"Your ninety seconds are going," Quill said.

"Open the shutter."

"No." Quill reached down, and the shutter dropped back against the chain with a bang that Sol felt in her teeth. Through the glass she watched the warden uncap a pen, pull the chained book toward the lantern, find a line near the top of the page, and draw one clean stroke through the name of the boat.

Sol got her fingers into the gap before the hasp settled.
